entities.name: Grand Mosque of Paris
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Grand Mosque of Paris (Grande Mosquée de Paris) is the largest mosque in France and one of the most historically significant mosques in the Western world, inaugurated in 1926 as a gift from the French government to the Muslim soldiers — primarily from Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, Senegal, and other French colonies — who died fighting for France in World War I. Over 500,000 Muslim soldiers fought for France; approximately 100,000 died.

The mosque was built in Hispano-Moorish style inspired by the Bou Inania Madrasa in Fez, Morocco, featuring geometric tile work, carved plasterwork, and a 33-meter minaret. The architect Robert Fournez and Algerian artisans created the complex including the mosque, gardens, hammam (Turkish bath), restaurant, and café over seven years (1919-1926). President Gaston Doumergue inaugurated it in the presence of the Sultan of Morocco.

The Grand Mosque's history reflects Franco-Muslim relations: during World War II occupation, French police records indicate the mosque's rector Si Kaddour Benghabrit issued certificates of Muslim identity to protect hundreds of Jews from deportation — an act of Muslim-Jewish solidarity that inspired the 2011 novel 'The Avenue of the Giants' (A'Ali Si Benghabrit). France's 5-6 million Muslim community — Europe's largest — has grown far beyond what the 1926 mosque symbolically represented, and debates over mosque building permits, Islamic schools, and the hijab reflect ongoing tensions in French-Muslim relations.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Grand Mosque of Paris, built to honor Muslim WWI soldiers who died for France, is the most historically charged mosque in the Western world — embodying colonial history, Muslim sacrifice, WWII resistance, and contemporary debates about Islam in Europe.
